blocks.text: A woman of 41 has had 'penicillin allergy' on every drug chart since a childhood rash that appeared during a viral illness. For three decades she has been given alternative antibiotics that are broader in spectrum, sometimes less effective and sometimes more toxic. The label was never checked. Deciding what an adverse reaction really was, and recording it accurately, is a core prescribing skill.

blocks.markdown:
An **adverse drug reaction (ADR)** is a noxious, unintended response to a medicine given at doses normally used in people. It is a subset of **adverse drug events**, which include any harm during treatment whether or not the drug caused it (for example a fall in an older patient who has just started an antihypertensive, which may or may not be causal). Reactions are grouped by **mechanism**, because the mechanism tells you whether the reaction was predictable, whether dose adjustment will help, and whether the patient must avoid the drug for life.

The classic Rawlins and Thompson scheme has two main groups. **Type A (augmented)** reactions are exaggerations of the drug's known pharmacology. **Type B (bizarre)** reactions are unrelated to the known pharmacology and are idiosyncratic or immunological. Later extensions add **Type C** (chronic or cumulative exposure), **Type D** (delayed, such as effects appearing long after exposure) and **Type E** (end of use, such as withdrawal).

blocks.title: ADR, side effect, intolerance, allergy
blocks.text: ADR: any harmful, unintended response at normal doses. Side effect: a predictable pharmacological effect, which may be harmful or harmless. Intolerance: a predictable, non-immune unpleasant effect (such as nausea with an opioid) that does not carry the risk of anaphylaxis. Allergy: an immune-mediated hypersensitivity reaction that occurs after prior sensitisation. Idiosyncratic: an unpredictable reaction not explained by the drug's known pharmacology, which may or may not be immune-mediated.

rows: Immunological or idiosyncratic; not explained by the drug's main action
Hypoglycaemia with a sulfonylurea; sedation with an opioid
Anaphylaxis to a penicillin; hypersensitivity syndrome with allopurinol
Reduce dose or alter regimen; check for interactions or impaired clearance
Stop the drug, usually avoid it in future, record the reaction
blocks.caption: Type A and Type B reactions compared. Exact frequencies vary by drug and population.

blocks.markdown: Quantifying harm helps put a predictable reaction in proportion. The **absolute risk increase (ARI)** is the event rate on the drug minus the event rate on the comparator. The **number needed to harm (NNH)** is the number of patients who must be treated for one additional patient to be harmed. For example, an adverse event rate of 3% on a drug against 1% on comparator gives ARI = 0.02 and NNH = 50.

blocks.caption: r is the event rate expressed as a proportion (0.03, not 3). NNH is conventionally rounded up to a whole patient in reports.

blocks.markdown: **Drug allergy** is classified by the Gell and Coombs scheme according to the immune mechanism. The timing of the reaction after exposure is the single most useful clue. **Type I** reactions are IgE-mediated and happen within minutes to about an hour. **Type II** reactions are antibody-mediated cytotoxic reactions (for example drug-induced haemolytic anaemia). **Type III** reactions are immune-complex mediated (serum sickness-like illness, typically one to two weeks after exposure). **Type IV** reactions are T-cell mediated and delayed, appearing from days to weeks later; they include maculopapular rashes, DRESS (drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms), and the severe skin reactions Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis.

rows: Maculopapular rash, DRESS, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis
blocks.caption: Gell and Coombs classification of drug hypersensitivity. Overlap occurs and timing is approximate.

blocks.markdown:
**Evaluating a reported allergy** means turning a label into facts. Ask: which drug (and which brand or class); when; what exactly happened (hives, swelling, wheeze, collapse, blistering, or only nausea); how soon after the dose; whether treatment such as adrenaline or admission was needed; whether the drug or a related one has been taken since without problems; and whether the history is from the patient or only hearsay. A family history of allergy does not make the patient allergic. Many patients labelled penicillin-allergic are not truly allergic on formal assessment, and an inaccurate label leads to broader-spectrum alternatives and avoidable harm.

**Cross-reactivity** is when a patient sensitised to one drug reacts to a structurally similar one. Within the beta-lactams, cross-reactivity between penicillins and cephalosporins is generally low and is driven mainly by similarity of the side chains (R1 groups) rather than the shared beta-lactam ring. Amoxicillin, ampicillin, cefalexin and cefadroxil share similar side chains. Current BNF guidance advises avoiding cephalosporins in people with a history of immediate hypersensitivity to penicillins; check the current BNF and local policy because advice is refined over time.

blocks.title: Evaluating an old 'penicillin allergy' label
blocks.prompt: A 45-year-old man needs antibiotics for cellulitis. His notes say 'penicillin allergy' with no detail. He says he was told as a toddler that he had 'come out in a rash' with a liquid antibiotic during a fever, and he has never taken a penicillin since. He needed no treatment for the rash. Evaluate the label.

steps.text: Gather the specifics. Drug: an unnamed penicillin liquid. Timing and features: a rash during a febrile illness, with no urticaria, swelling, wheeze or collapse reported, and no treatment needed. Nothing suggests an immediate (Type I) reaction.

Interpret the pattern. Non-urticarial rashes in children given antibiotics during viral infections are common and often the infection, not the drug. This history is low-risk but it is old, second-hand and incomplete, so it is not proof of tolerance.

Decide the safe action. Do not delete the label on history alone. Follow the local penicillin allergy pathway or take microbiology or pharmacy advice on whether a penicillin can be given, with monitoring, or whether a non-penicillin alternative is appropriate. Check the current BNF and local guidance for the drug and regimen.

Document the outcome. Record the details in the allergy field (drug, year, reaction, certainty), and consider referral for formal penicillin allergy assessment so the label can be confirmed or removed.

blocks.answer: The label is low-risk on history but unverified. Record the detail, use the local pathway for the immediate decision, and refer for formal de-labelling rather than guessing.

blocks.title: Labelling intolerance as allergy
blocks.text: Recording nausea, diarrhoea or drowsiness as an 'allergy' removes a drug from the formulary of options for no good reason, and it hides true allergies among false ones. Record intolerances as side effects, with the drug, the symptom and whether it was severe, and keep the allergy field for reactions that are plausibly immune-mediated.

blocks.markdown: **Reporting.** In the UK, suspected ADRs are reported to the MHRA through the **Yellow Card scheme**, online or through the Yellow Card app. Healthcare professionals and patients and carers can all report. You do not need to be certain the drug caused the event; suspicion is enough. Report all suspected reactions to medicines carrying the **black triangle** (additional monitoring, such as newer medicines and biological products), all suspected reactions in children and to vaccines, and all **serious** reactions to established medicines (fatal, life-threatening, disabling, causing a congenital abnormality, requiring or prolonging hospital stay, or medically significant). Include the suspect drug (brand and batch where known), dose, route, dates, the reaction and its outcome, other medicines including over-the-counter and herbal products, and the reporter's details. Check the current MHRA guidance for the reporting criteria.

blocks.title: Classify three events and decide on reporting
blocks.prompt: A ward pharmacist reviews three events. Event 1: a patient starting metformin has loose stools in the first week that settle. Event 2: a woman develops cholestatic jaundice three weeks after finishing a course of flucloxacillin. Event 3: a patient on a newly licensed black-triangle medicine has a mild headache after the first dose. Classify each and decide what to do.

steps.text: Event 1: gastrointestinal upset with metformin is a well-known, frequent, dose-related effect of its pharmacology, and it settles. This is a Type A reaction (or intolerance) and is not serious. Record it and counsel; a Yellow Card is not routinely needed for an established medicine unless serious.

Event 2: jaundice appearing after the course has ended does not follow the dose and cannot be predicted from flucloxacillin's antibacterial pharmacology. It is an idiosyncratic Type B reaction with a delayed onset, and it is serious (hepatic injury, likely admission). The time gap does not exclude the drug; flucloxacillin cholestasis can present after treatment has stopped.
Action for event 2: record the reaction in the allergy and adverse reaction section so the drug is not re-prescribed, inform the patient and the GP, and submit a Yellow Card because it is serious.
Event 3: for a black-triangle medicine all suspected reactions are reportable, however mild, because the safety profile is still being built. Submit a Yellow Card even though causality is uncertain.

blocks.answer: Event 1 is a Type A effect needing no report; event 2 is a serious Type B reaction to report and record; event 3 is reportable because of the black triangle.

items: Say what the drug was, what happened and when it began relative to the dose.
Classify: predictable pharmacology (Type A), unpredictable (Type B), or chronic, delayed or end-of-use (C to E).
Judge whether it looks immune-mediated, and which type from the timing and features.
Record accurately in the allergy and adverse reaction field, distinguishing allergy from intolerance.
Tell the patient and the next clinician, and report via the Yellow Card scheme where criteria are met.

points: Type A reactions are dose-related and predictable from the drug's pharmacology; Type B reactions are unpredictable, usually not dose-related and often serious.
Gell and Coombs types I to IV link immune mechanism to timing: immediate IgE reactions occur within about an hour, delayed T-cell reactions take days to weeks.
Evaluate an allergy label by establishing the drug, timing, features, treatment needed and later tolerance; intolerance should not be recorded as allergy.
Penicillin-cephalosporin cross-reactivity is low and mainly side-chain related, but avoid cephalosporins after immediate penicillin hypersensitivity unless guidance supports otherwise.
Report suspected ADRs to the MHRA Yellow Card scheme; suspicion is enough, and black-triangle drugs, children, vaccines and serious reactions are priorities.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a Type A (augmented) adverse drug reaction?
questions.explanation: Type A reactions are the commonest ADRs and are predictable because they arise from the drug's own pharmacology. They usually respond to dose reduction or removing a cause such as impaired clearance.

options.text: An unpredictable reaction unrelated to the drug's pharmacology
An exaggerated effect of the drug's known pharmacology that is usually dose-related
A reaction that appears only after sensitisation by a previous dose
A reaction that occurs only when the drug is stopped

questions.correctOptionText: An exaggerated effect of the drug's known pharmacology that is usually dose-related

distractorRationale.b: Correct: Type A reactions extend the known pharmacological action and are dose-related.
distractorRationale.c: Sensitisation is characteristic of allergic (immunological Type B) reactions.
distractorRationale.d: This describes end-of-use (Type E) reactions, such as withdrawal.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best example of a Type B (idiosyncratic or immunological) reaction?
questions.explanation: Type B reactions cannot be predicted from the drug's pharmacology and are not reliably dose-related. Prior uneventful exposure fits sensitisation, which then produces an immediate reaction on later exposure.

options.text: Dry mouth in a patient taking an antimuscarinic drug
Hypoglycaemia after an insulin dose is increased
Urticaria, wheeze and hypotension within minutes of re-exposure to a drug taken uneventfully before
Drowsiness after a higher dose of an opioid

questions.correctOptionText: Urticaria, wheeze and hypotension within minutes of re-exposure to a drug taken uneventfully before

distractorRationale.a: This follows directly from the antimuscarinic action, so it is Type A.
distractorRationale.b: This is an exaggeration of insulin's glucose-lowering effect, so it is Type A.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: an immediate reaction on re-exposure after earlier uneventful use is typical of IgE-mediated sensitisation, which is not predictable from the drug's pharmacology.
distractorRationale.d: Sedation is an expected, dose-related opioid effect, so it is Type A.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old has documented anaphylaxis (urticaria, wheeze and collapse within 10 minutes) after amoxicillin two years ago. She now needs an antibiotic for a chest infection. Which approach is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Immediate-type (Type I) reactions carry the risk of anaphylaxis on re-exposure, so conservative avoidance is needed. Check current BNF and local policy, and involve microbiology or allergy services where options are limited.

options.text: Prescribe a cephalosporin because cross-reactivity with penicillins is negligible
Prescribe a different penicillin because the reaction was to amoxicillin only
Avoid penicillins, and avoid cephalosporins unless guidance or specialist advice supports them; choose from alternative classes and check BNF and local policy
Ignore the history because the reaction was two years ago

questions.correctOptionText: Avoid penicillins, and avoid cephalosporins unless guidance or specialist advice supports them; choose from alternative classes and check BNF and local policy

distractorRationale.a: Cross-reactivity is low rather than absent, and BNF advises avoiding cephalosporins after immediate hypersensitivity to penicillins.
distractorRationale.b: Other penicillins share the core structure and the reaction was immediate and severe, so another penicillin is unsafe.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: an immediate severe reaction means avoiding penicillins and, unless specialist advice supports it, cephalosporins.
distractorRationale.d: IgE-mediated sensitisation can persist for years, and a time gap does not make re-exposure safe.

questions.stem: Which suspected reaction should always be reported to the Yellow Card scheme?
questions.explanation: The Yellow Card scheme depends on suspicion. Serious reactions, reactions to black-triangle medicines, vaccines and reactions in children are particular priorities.

options.text: Only reactions where the causal link is proven
Only reactions in hospital inpatients
Only reactions reported by doctors
A suspected serious reaction to an established medicine, even if causality is uncertain

questions.correctOptionText: A suspected serious reaction to an established medicine, even if causality is uncertain

distractorRationale.a: Suspicion is enough; waiting for proof defeats the purpose of signal detection.
distractorRationale.b: Reports are accepted from any setting, including primary care and the community.
distractorRationale.c: Patients, carers and other healthcare professionals can also report.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: serious suspected reactions should be reported, and certainty about causality is not required.

questions.stem: A patient reports 'allergy to codeine' because it makes her feel sick and constipated. How should this be recorded?
questions.explanation: Misclassifying intolerance as allergy removes useful drugs from consideration and hides genuine allergies. Accurate descriptions help the next prescriber decide what is safe.

options.text: As a true drug allergy, so that all opioids are avoided
It should not be recorded because it is only a side effect
As an intolerance or side effect, with the drug, the symptoms and their severity, not as an allergy
As a Type IV hypersensitivity reaction

questions.correctOptionText: As an intolerance or side effect, with the drug, the symptoms and their severity, not as an allergy

distractorRationale.a: Nausea and constipation are expected opioid effects, not immune-mediated, so labelling as allergy is misleading.
distractorRationale.b: Omitting it risks the same unpleasant effect being repeated; it should be recorded accurately.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: record a predictable non-immune effect as an intolerance with the details.
distractorRationale.d: Nothing in the history suggests T-cell mediated hypersensitivity.

questions.stem: True or false: a drug allergy is an immune-mediated reaction, whereas drug intolerance is a predictable non-immune effect of the drug.
questions.explanation: Allergy requires an immune mechanism and prior sensitisation, and can be severe or life-threatening. Intolerance reflects the drug's pharmacological effects, such as nausea, and is not immune-mediated.

options.text: True
False

questions.stem: In a trial of a new drug, 6.5% of 800 patients taking it developed a particular ADR, against 2.0% of 800 patients on the comparator. Calculate the number needed to harm (NNH) as a number of patients, to one decimal place.
questions.explanation: The absolute risk increase is 0.065 minus 0.020, which is 0.045. NNH is the reciprocal, 1 divided by 0.045, which is about 22.2, so around 22 patients must be treated for one additional person to be harmed.

questions.stem: Describe how a healthcare professional should report a suspected adverse drug reaction in the UK, and what information the report should contain.
questions.explanation: A good answer names the Yellow Card scheme and states that suspicion is sufficient. It then lists the data that make a report useful and mentions local documentation, so the reaction is visible to future prescribers.
markingGuide: Report to the MHRA via the Yellow Card scheme (website or app); patients and carers can also report
Suspicion of causality is enough; certainty is not required
Priority reports: serious reactions to established medicines, all suspected reactions to black-triangle medicines, vaccines and reactions in children
Content: suspect drug (brand, batch where known), dose, route, start and stop dates, reaction description, onset and outcome
Content: other medicines including over-the-counter and herbal, relevant patient details, reporter details
Also document the reaction in the notes and allergy record, inform the patient and use local incident reporting where relevant

questions.stem: A 19-year-old develops widespread urticaria and lip swelling about 20 minutes after taking the second dose of oral cefalexin prescribed for a skin infection. She has previously taken amoxicillin without problems. Evaluate the reaction and explain the implications for future prescribing and documentation.
questions.explanation: The key is to recognise the immediate mechanism, document it precisely and recognise side-chain cross-reactivity. Earlier tolerance of amoxicillin does not clear the penicillin class because the allergy may relate to the shared side chain and tolerance can change.
markingGuide: Immediate onset with urticaria and angioedema suggests a Type I IgE-mediated reaction, appearing on the second dose consistent with sensitisation
Treat as a true allergy, record the drug, features, timing and severity
Cefalexin shares a similar side chain with amoxicillin and ampicillin, so cross-reactivity with those penicillins cannot be excluded despite earlier tolerance of amoxicillin
Until assessed, avoid cefalexin and consider avoiding penicillins and cephalosporins with similar side chains, following BNF and local policy
Use a non-beta-lactam alternative if antibiotics are needed and refer to an allergy service for formal assessment
Inform the patient, update the allergy record, and report via the Yellow Card scheme if the criteria are met

questions.stem: Compare the following two reactions. (i) A 78-year-old on regular morphine, whose dose has been increased, becomes drowsy and constipated. (ii) A 40-year-old develops fever, widespread rash and abnormal liver tests five weeks after starting allopurinol. Classify each, explain the likely mechanism and state how the response differs.
questions.explanation: The two cases show why classification matters in practice: a predictable dose-related effect is managed by adjustment, whereas a serious idiosyncratic hypersensitivity needs withdrawal and lifelong avoidance. Timing and features guide the classification.
markingGuide: (i) Type A: exaggerated, dose-related pharmacological effect of an opioid, predictable
(i) Response: review dose, consider renal function and interacting sedatives, treat constipation, monitor; the drug may often be continued at an adjusted dose
(ii) Type B: delayed (Type IV, T-cell mediated) hypersensitivity, for example DRESS, not predicted by pharmacology and not dose-related
(ii) Response: stop the drug, supportive and specialist management, do not rechallenge, record as an allergy
Inform the patient, document, and report via the Yellow Card scheme (serious reaction)
Overall contrast: Type A is managed by adjusting dose and cause, Type B by stopping and avoiding
